title: SYSK Selects: Sugar: It Powers the Earth
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the episode on sugar. The hosts trace sugar's history from its probable origin in New Guinea and Polynesia through India, the Persians, the Crusades, and Columbus's introduction of sugarcane to the Caribbean. They cover sugar's early luxury status, Venetian trade with England in 1319, the Reformation's effect on honey, the rise of tea drinking in Britain, and the sugar beet in the 1700s. The episode explains how sugarcane and sugar beets are processed into crystals, including centrifuges, mother liquor, molasses, and bagasse, and mentions the Savannah sugar refinery explosion. It compares sugar types (sucrose, glucose, fructose, lactose, xylitol, table, castor, icing, and preserving sugar), and discusses high fructose corn syrup and its liver metabolism, sugar's role in tooth decay, insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes, and sugar-based ethanol in Brazil and microbial fuel cells. The episode closes with a listener mail rebuttal about micro- and macroevolution.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts open with jokes about sweet terms of endearment and the Archies song, plus a tease about a future Simpsons-style episode.

segments.title: Sugar origins and spread
segments.summary: Sugar is thought to have originated in New Guinea and spread through Polynesia, Indonesia, and India. The Persians, the Crusades, and Columbus carried it to Western Europe and the Caribbean.

segments.title: Sugar as a luxury and the Venetian trade
segments.summary: Sugar was a royal luxury early on. Venice sold fifty tons to England in 1319. The Reformation closed monasteries and reduced honey production while sugar became cheaper, which helped drive tea drinking in Britain.

segments.title: Sugar beets and the Napoleonic-era blockades
segments.summary: Naval blockades during the European wars created demand for alternatives. In 1747 the sugar beet was identified as a source, and it remains a major source of sugar today. Hosts compare beet and cane sugar yields.

segments.title: Sugar processing: cane and beet
segments.summary: Sugar beets and sugarcane are both boiled into a sugary juice, filtered, and spun in a centrifuge to separate crystals from mother liquor. Sugar dust is sometimes added to spur crystallization. The hosts discuss the Savannah sugar refinery explosion caused by airborne sugar dust.

segments.title: Byproducts: molasses, rum, bagasse
segments.summary: Molasses is a byproduct of boiling sugar, and it gives brown sugar its color. Rum is made from molasses. Bagasse, the fibrous pulp left from cane, is burned as fuel to power refineries, though mass production still causes deforestation.

segments.title: Types of sugar
segments.summary: The hosts describe sucrose, glucose, fructose, lactose, and galactose. They also cover xylitol, a sugar alcohol that does not affect blood sugar, and granulated, castor, icing, and preserving sugar.

segments.title: Ice cream tangent and simple syrup
segments.summary: Hosts digress into Bluebell ice cream and personal favorites, then discuss simple syrup and its use as a preservative.

segments.title: High fructose corn syrup and the liver
segments.summary: High fructose corn syrup is roughly similar to sucrose, but fructose is processed by the liver and can be converted to fat. Hosts discuss the New York Times article on sugar toxicity and the USDA's added-sugar guidance. They cite US and global per-person sugar consumption figures.

segments.title: Sugar, taste, plants, and teeth
segments.summary: Sugar's sweet taste comes from how its molecules fit taste receptors. Plants make sugar through photosynthesis and use it in nectar to attract pollinators. Bacteria such as Streptococcus mutans feed on sugar and produce lactic acid that erodes tooth enamel.

segments.title: Sugar, insulin, and diabetes
segments.summary: Excess sugar can cause insulin resistance and metabolic syndrome, which may drive obesity and heart disease. Type 2 diabetes results when the pancreas is overtaxed. Hosts compare this with earlier fat-focused diet theories.

segments.title: Sugar as fuel: ethanol and microbial fuel cells
segments.summary: Brazil ran heavily on sugarcane ethanol, though cheaper gasoline later reduced its use. Competition for sugar can raise food prices and harm workers. Microbes that eat sugar can release electrons to create electricity, producing water as a byproduct.

segments.title: Listener mail: evolution rebuttal
segments.summary: A listener rebuttal argues that micro- and macroevolution describe the same natural selection process over different timescales, in response to an earlier creationist listener email.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listener contributions and mention website and social channels.
